claims.text: Conventional stainless or Fe–Cr steel forms a chromium-rich passive oxide film under service conditions.
A chromium-rich passive oxide layer is the primary cause of corrosion resistance in steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
The chromium-rich passive film forms rapidly and is self-healing.
Severe plastic deformation produces an ultrafine-grained steel with increased grain-boundary density.
Grain boundaries in ultrafine-grained steel act as fast diffusion pathways for chromium atoms.
Accelerated grain-boundary chromium transport produces a thicker and more uniform Cr2O3 passive film.
After local film damage, high grain-boundary density promotes prompt chromium segregation and reformation of the protective oxide.
A dense Cr2O3 passivation film suppresses corrosion.
Aqueous chloride or acidified solutions near 300°C are representative test environments for both chemical-processing and nuclear-power service.
Ultrafine-grained steel will form a Cr-enriched passive film faster and more completely than coarse-grained steel.
Ultrafine-grained steel will exhibit lower corrosion current density than coarse-grained steel under identical conditions.
Ultrafine-grained steel will exhibit reduced pit initiation and growth relative to coarse-grained steel.
Coarse-grained stainless steel has moderate corrosion rates under the proposed test conditions.
Chromium contents above approximately 10 wt% are sufficient for the proposed passivation mechanism.
The grain-boundary diffusion mechanism remains effective in moderately aggressive aqueous environments up to about 300°C.
At very high temperatures or under atypical chemical exposures, factors other than chromium passivation and grain-boundary diffusion may dominate corrosion.
